title: 2027 Conforming Loan Limits: What SoCal Buyers Need to Know
description: FHFA raised the 2027 conforming loan limit to $855,400 and $1,283,100 in high-cost areas. Here's what it means for Southern California homebuyers.
image_alt: Aerial view of red-roofed homes and tree-lined streets in a small California town

faq.q: What is the conforming loan limit for 2027?
faq.a: FHFA set the 2027 baseline conforming loan limit for one-unit homes at $855,400, with a high-cost area ceiling of $1,283,100. The new limits apply starting January 1, 2027.

faq.q: What is the 2027 conforming loan limit in Orange County or Los Angeles?
faq.a: Los Angeles and Orange counties have been at the high-cost ceiling, which rises to $1,283,100 for one-unit homes in 2027. Confirm your county's exact figure on FHFA's official county list.

faq.q: Is a loan above the conforming limit a jumbo loan?
faq.a: Yes. A loan amount above the conforming limit for the county where the home is located is generally a jumbo loan, with guidelines set by each lender or investor.

body_html:
Here's a question I hear every winter: "If I wait until January, can I borrow more without going jumbo?" This year the answer matters more than usual for Southern California buyers, because the line between a conforming loan and a jumbo loan just moved.

On November 24, 2026, the Federal Housing Finance Agency announced the 2027 conforming loan limits for loans Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can buy. Here's what changed, what it means if you're shopping in Los Angeles, Orange, San Diego, Riverside or San Bernardino County, and how to use the new numbers in your planning.

What FHFA announced for 2027

According to FHFA's announcement, as also reported by the National Association of Home Builders, the baseline conforming loan limit for a one-unit home rises to $855,400 in 2027, up $22,650 from $832,750 in 2026. That's an increase of about 2.7%, tied to the change in FHFA's House Price Index between the third quarters of 2025 and 2026.

In high-cost areas, the ceiling is 150% of the baseline, which puts it at $1,283,100 for a one-unit home, up from $1,249,125. FHFA said limits will be higher in all but 24 U.S. counties. The new limits apply to loans delivered to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac starting January 1, 2027.

One thing worth knowing: the increase is a bit smaller than last year's, which reflects slower home price growth nationally. It's still a meaningful bump for buyers sitting right on the edge.

Why the conforming line matters so much

A conforming loan is one that fits Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac's size limits and guidelines. Anything above the limit for your county is a jumbo loan, and each lender or investor sets its own jumbo rules. I covered those differences in detail in Jumbo Loans in Southern California: What's Different, but the short version looks like this:

FactorConforming loanJumbo loan
GuidelinesStandardized by Fannie Mae and Freddie MacSet by each lender or investor
ReservesOften lighter requirementsOften several months of payments in the bank
Credit expectationsBroad range of profiles acceptedTypically stricter
AppraisalUsually one appraisalSometimes two on larger loans
DocumentationFamiliar, predictable checklistCan be more detailed

Jumbo financing isn't bad. Plenty of Southern California buyers use it successfully. But a conforming loan usually means more predictable underwriting and more flexibility on reserves and credit. When a higher limit pulls your loan back under the line, that can make the whole process simpler.

What it means county by county in Southern California

Conforming limits are set county by county, and Southern California spans several tiers:

  • Los Angeles and Orange counties have been at the high-cost ceiling. If they stay there in 2027, the one-unit limit would be the new $1,283,100 maximum.
  • San Diego and Ventura counties have had their own high-cost limits that sit between the baseline and the ceiling, based on local median values.
  • Riverside and San Bernardino counties have been at the baseline. If they stay there, their one-unit limit rises to $855,400.

Don't rely on a blog post (including this one) for your county's exact figure. FHFA publishes the official county-by-county list, including limits for two- to four-unit properties, on its conforming loan limit page. Before you set a price range, look up the county where the home is located, not the county where you live today.

Who benefits most from the higher limit

The new limit doesn't change what a home costs or what you can afford on your income. What it changes is which loan category your purchase falls into. A few situations where that makes a real difference:

  • Buyers right at the edge. If your planned loan amount sits just above the 2026 limit, the 2027 limit may put it back in conforming territory, depending on your county.
  • Move-up buyers in the Inland Empire. Riverside and San Bernardino homes have been creeping toward the baseline. A higher baseline gives a little more room before jumbo rules kick in.
  • Buyers of two- to four-unit properties. Multi-unit limits rise too, which can help house hackers and multigenerational households. Check FHFA's list for those figures.
  • Homeowners thinking about a refinance. If your current loan is a jumbo and your balance now fits under the new limit, it may be worth a conversation about whether a conforming refinance makes sense for you. My guide on when refinancing makes sense walks through how to think about it.

Timing: should you wait until January?

Here's where I'd be careful. Some lenders began offering loan amounts above the 2026 limit earlier this fall based on their own expectations, and FHFA's official numbers are now out. But each lender decides when it will start accepting the new limits, and your closing timeline matters too.

If you're house hunting in December and your loan would land between the old and new limit, ask your lender three questions:

  • Are you accepting loans at the 2027 limit now, or only for loans closing or delivered after January 1?
  • If my loan is above the 2026 limit today, how would it be underwritten if we close in December versus January?
  • Does my county's 2027 limit cover my planned loan amount, including any financed fees?

Waiting for a loan limit isn't a reason to lose the right house, and rushing isn't a reason to take on a structure you don't need. The goal is to know your options before you write an offer, so you and your agent can plan around them.

FHA loan limits are a separate set of numbers that HUD announces on its own schedule. They're based on the conforming limits, but they're not the same, so if you're considering FHA, confirm that program's limit for your county separately. My FHA vs. conventional comparison can help you decide which path fits.

The takeaway

The 2027 conforming loan limit rises to $855,400 in baseline counties and $1,283,100 in the highest-cost areas, per FHFA. For Southern California buyers near the jumbo line, that can mean simpler underwriting and more flexibility. Look up the official figure for the county where you're buying, check how your lender is handling the transition, and build your price range around the loan category you actually want to be in.
